target: AG1’s claim that making Election Day a national holiday would broadly reduce work-based barriers to voting for low-income workers
objection: A federal national holiday does not require private employers to give paid time off or close, so many low-income retail and service workers would still be scheduled to work during polling hours and would not receive meaningful relief.

target: AG1’s assumption that a national holiday would reliably improve turnout enough to justify the policy
objection: Research indicates that an election holiday by itself is not an effective turnout strategy compared with other voting-access reforms, so the holiday is an ineffective way to raise participation.

target: AG2’s claim that a federal holiday would fail to help low-income workers because private employers may still operate
objection: Even if some private employers remain open, a national holiday typically changes scheduling patterns enough that many low-income retail and service workers are less likely to be scheduled for their usual Election Day hours, so the holiday would still reduce work-based conflicts for many.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday is ineffective if it does not solve every worker’s conflict
objection: The policy does not need to eliminate all conflicts for every person to be justified; it is enough that it materially reduces barriers for many voters and also elevates voting as a civic event.

target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday would also solve school-based voting barriers
objection: A federal holiday does not automatically change K-12 school calendars, because school closures are set by state and local authorities, so school-day obligations may continue despite federal holiday status.

target: AG1’s claim that school-based conflicts would therefore be removed for students and school-dependent households
objection: If schools are not reliably paused, then school-based scheduling conflicts would often persist during polling hours and the holiday would not reliably remove that barrier.

target: AG2’s claim that school-related barriers are unaffected because schools may stay open
objection: Even if schools do not all close, a federal holiday still changes many employers’ staffing patterns and can ease guardians’ work schedules, which helps school-dependent households vote during polling hours.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday only works if every school obligation disappears
objection: School obligations need not vanish completely for the holiday to help; easing guardians’ work schedules can make school-related constraints less likely to block voting in school-dependent households.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday reliably gives low-income workers time off
objection: Federal holiday status does not legally require private employers to close or provide paid time off, so many low-income workers can still be scheduled to work and may not get any reliable time off to vote.

target: AG1’s claim that the holiday meaningfully helps school-dependent households through guardians’ eased work schedules
objection: Many low-income parents in retail and service jobs still work holiday shifts that overlap polling hours, so the work conflict can persist even if school constraints are reduced.

target: AG1’s justification that the holiday is good even without guaranteeing every worker time off
objection: A policy should not be justified mainly by benefits that do not reliably reach the least-flexible low-income voters, especially when the work-based conflict often remains.

target: AG1’s view that variable state reforms are inferior because they are not nationwide
objection: State voting-leave laws can create an enforceable entitlement to time off for voting, making access more dependable than a federal holiday that relies on employer discretion.

target: AG2’s claim that state voting-leave rules are sufficient because they are enforceable
objection: State voting-leave rules address employer-related work conflicts, but they do not solve school-day obligations for students and school-dependent households, whereas a national holiday addresses both work and school scheduling barriers.

target: AG1’s claim that a federal holiday will reduce work-based barriers for low-income workers
objection: A federal holiday does not legally force private employers to grant paid time off or stop staffing, so many low-income retail and service workers would still have shifts during polling hours and would not reliably get relief.

target: AG1’s claim that reduced school obligations offset the holiday’s weaknesses for low-income households
objection: If work conflicts persist for many low-income workers, then reduced school obligations do not translate into reliable voting access for the people with the least flexibility.

target: AG2’s claim that a national holiday is ineffective or inequitable because it lacks a guaranteed PTO entitlement
objection: The holiday should be judged by whether it broadly reduces scheduling overlap in practice, not by whether it creates a perfect enforceable PTO entitlement for every individual.

target: AG1’s reliance on OECD weekend/holiday election examples to defend the policy
objection: Holiday-based election scheduling may work in some democracies, but the U.S. context is different because the holiday does not compel private employers to close or provide paid leave, so those international examples do not show the policy is effective here.

target: AG2’s claim that state-level reforms are more reliable than a national holiday
objection: State-level reforms are unevenly implemented across states, so they do not guarantee consistent voting-time accommodations for all low-income voters nationwide the way a federal holiday can provide a uniform scheduling change.

target: AG1’s claim that a federal holiday would uniformly reduce scheduling barriers nationwide
objection: A federal holiday does not reliably change private-employer staffing or paid leave across employers, so the supposed uniform nationwide relief does not actually hold for low-income workers.

target: AG2’s claim that holiday-driven schedule changes are too uneven to matter
objection: A federal holiday still creates broad nationwide expectations that ripple into real scheduling practices, producing practical schedule shifts and reduced overlap with polling hours for many voters.

target: AG1’s claim that civic celebration can offset practical shortcomings of the holiday
objection: Making voting feel like a civic celebration does not create time for people who still must work during polling hours, so civic framing cannot substitute for actual access.

target: AG2’s overall claim that only a perfect guarantee of time off makes the holiday justified
objection: The policy is justified if it reduces the main scheduling barriers for many voters and strengthens civic participation, even if it does not guarantee a perfect entitlement in every workplace.
